questions.stem: How are peripheral arterial bypass grafts named?
questions.answer: By where the bypass starts and ends

questions.stem: Which conduits are used for bypass grafts in peripheral arterial bypass surgery?
options: Short saphenous vein or pericardial patch
Long saphenous vein or synthetic graft
Internal jugular vein or cadaveric artery

In peripheral arterial bypass, which patient group needs particular anaesthetic attention?
questions.answer: Vascular patients with systemic arterial disease

questions.stem: How is peripheral arterial bypass usually tolerated compared with aortic surgery?
options: Not comparable, as the risks differ widely

questions.stem: Before peripheral arterial bypass, when is dynamic cardiac testing needed?
options: Only for patients with a pacemaker
Rarely, unless something new such as unstable angina

options: At least one large IV cannula (14 or 16G)

questions.stem: Where do stable patients go after peripheral arterial bypass?

options: Those with fit healthy hearts and no comorbidities
Those with comorbidities such as heart failure
Patients who had a short operation under 1hr

questions.stem: What is the graft route in axillo-bifemoral bypass?
options: Intraperitoneal graft from aorta to both iliac arteries
Extraperitoneal trouser graft from axillary artery to both femoral arteries
Retroperitoneal graft from abdominal aorta to popliteal artery
Subcutaneous graft from carotid artery to both femoral arteries

questions.stem: How does axillo-bifemoral bypass compare with open AAA repair?
options: More invasive and shorter in duration
Less invasive and better tolerated, but very long

questions.stem: When is axillo-bifemoral bypass indicated?
options: Mild femoropopliteal disease in young fit patients
Isolated tibial disease in patients with diabetes
Severe aorto-iliac occlusive disease in patients too frail for open aortic surgery
Acute limb ischaemia in fit younger adults
